title: Student Loan Repayment Plans 2026: RAP vs Tiered Standard
description: US federal student loan repayment in 2026: how RAP and the Tiered Standard plan work, what SAVE borrowers must do, and which plan fits a first salary.

cover.alt: A graduation cap resting on a stack of papers

keywords: student loan repayment plans 2026 RAP repayment assistance plan tiered standard plan SAVE plan ended
takeaways: SAVE has ended. New federal loans from July 1, 2026 can use only RAP or the Tiered Standard plan.
RAP sets your payment from your income. Tiered Standard sets a fixed payment from your balance.
Check your plan on StudentAid.gov. Older loans may still qualify for IBR, which can be cheaper.
body:
This guide covers federal student loans in the United States only. Private loans follow whatever contract you signed with your lender, and none of the plans below apply to them.

If you left school in 2026, or you had a loan sitting in the SAVE plan, your repayment plan may have changed this year without you picking anything. The SAVE plan has ended. Since July 1, 2026, new federal loans come with exactly two choices: the Repayment Assistance Plan, called RAP, which sets your payment from your income, and the Tiered Standard Plan, which sets a fixed payment from how much you owe.

If your loans are older, you still have more options for now, but two of them, PAYE and ICR, end on July 1, 2028.

Below: how to check which plan you are on, how the two new plans work, what each one costs on a low starting salary, and the dates not to miss.

## What actually changed in 2026

Congress rewrote the repayment menu in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, and Federal Student Aid has updated its official plan list to match.

SAVE is finished. The plan ended after a court approved a settlement between the Department of Education and the State of Missouri. The Department says about 7.5 million borrowers were enrolled in SAVE. From July 1, 2026, loan servicers began sending those borrowers notices giving them at least 90 days to pick a new plan. If a borrower does nothing, the servicer moves them onto the Standard plan or the new Tiered Standard plan automatically. Neither default looks at your income, so the payment can jump a lot.

For loans first paid out on or after July 1, 2026, the menu is just two plans: RAP or Tiered Standard.

For loans taken out before that date, the older income driven plans are still open: Income-Based Repayment (IBR), Pay As You Earn (PAYE), and Income-Contingent Repayment (ICR), and you can choose RAP too. One warning from Federal Student Aid is worth reading twice: if you take a first payout on a new loan on or after July 1, 2026, including a new consolidation loan, you lose access to IBR, ICR, and PAYE. A small new loan can quietly close doors on your old ones.

## First, check which plan you are on right now

Do not guess this. A lot of people are paying on a plan they never chose.

1. Log in at StudentAid.gov and open your dashboard. It lists each loan, when it was paid out, and who your servicer is. Those payout dates decide which plans you can use.
2. Open your servicer account and find the repayment plan name next to each loan. If it still says SAVE, or your loans sit in a forbearance tied to SAVE, you need to pick a new plan.
3. Read any letter or email from your servicer. Former SAVE borrowers get a deadline of at least 90 days, and your servicer will tell you your specific date.
4. If you were moved to Tiered Standard automatically and the payment does not fit your budget, you are not stuck. You can apply for an income driven plan on StudentAid.gov. Letting the site pull your tax information from the IRS, with your consent, makes the application faster.

While you sort this out, fit the payment into your monthly spending plan. If you do not have one yet, start with [how to budget on less than $1,000 a month](/blog/budget-on-less-than-1000-a-month/).

## The Tiered Standard Plan, in plain English

Tiered Standard is the fixed payment plan. Your payment is worked out from how much you owe and your interest rate. Your income plays no part in it, which makes it simple, and also unforgiving in a low paid month.

How long you get to repay depends on your total balance:

- Less than $25,000: 10 years
- $25,000 to $49,999: 15 years
- $50,000 to $99,999: 20 years
- $100,000 or more: 25 years

Your payment stays the same every month until the loan is gone. There is no yearly income paperwork, and there is no forgiveness at the end, because the schedule is built to pay the loan off in full.

Two things to know. First, this is the default. Federal Student Aid says that if you do not pick a plan, and your loan was paid out on or after July 1, 2026, your servicer puts you on Tiered Standard, including when you leave school. Second, a longer term cuts the monthly payment but adds interest. Stretching a balance over 20 or 25 years costs far more in total than clearing it in 10.

## The Repayment Assistance Plan (RAP), in plain English

RAP is the income driven plan. Instead of looking at your balance, it looks at your adjusted gross income, or AGI, which is the income figure from your federal tax return. If tax forms are new to you, [how to file taxes for the first time](/blog/file-taxes-first-time/) walks through the basics.

Your yearly payment is a percentage of your AGI, split into 12 monthly payments. The percentage rises in steps as your income rises:

| Your AGI              | Yearly amount used |
|-----------------------|--------------------|
| $10,000 or less      | $120 flat         |
| $10,001 to $20,000  | 1% of AGI          |
| $20,001 to $30,000  | 2% of AGI          |
| $30,001 to $40,000  | 3% of AGI          |
| $40,001 to $50,000  | 4% of AGI          |
| $50,001 to $60,000  | 5% of AGI          |
| $60,001 to $70,000  | 6% of AGI          |
| $70,001 to $80,000  | 7% of AGI          |
| $80,001 to $90,000  | 8% of AGI          |
| $90,001 to $100,000 | 9% of AGI          |
| Over $100,000        | 10% of AGI         |

From that amount, subtract $50 a month for each dependent you claim on your tax return. Whatever the math says, the payment never drops below $10 a month.

RAP also has two protections worth knowing about. If your payment does not cover the interest that built up that month, the leftover interest is covered for you, so your balance does not grow while you pay on time. And if your payment barely dents the amount you borrowed, the government adds a matching payment toward your principal of up to $50 a month.

If anything is left after 30 years of qualifying payments, that balance is forgiven. Forgiven amounts may count as taxable income, according to loan servicer Edfinancial, so it is not quite free money. RAP payments also count toward Public Service Loan Forgiveness, which clears the remaining balance after 120 qualifying payments if you work full time for a qualifying employer.

The one chore: you must update your income and family size every year, even if nothing changed. Federal Student Aid says you can agree to share your tax information so this yearly update happens automatically.

One hard limit: Parent PLUS loans cannot use RAP, and neither can a consolidation loan that includes a Parent PLUS loan.

## RAP vs Tiered Standard at a glance

|                               | RAP                               | Tiered Standard                    |
|-------------------------------|-----------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| How the payment is set        | A percentage of your income (AGI) | Your balance and interest rate     |
| Changes when your pay changes | Yes, checked every year           | No, fixed until payoff             |
| Yearly paperwork              | Yes, yearly income update         | None                               |
| If you never finish paying    | Balance forgiven after 30 years   | None; the schedule pays it in full |
| Can the balance grow?         | No, unpaid interest is covered    | No, it falls monthly by design     |
| Tends to suit                 | Low or uneven income              | Steady income, clear finish date   |

## What each plan costs on a first salary

The numbers below are an illustration with made up figures, so you can see how the two plans behave. They are not a quote for your loans.

Say you owe $28,000 in Direct Loans, all paid out after July 1, 2026, with a first job AGI of $32,000, no dependents, and a made up interest rate of 6 percent. Your take home pay will look smaller than that salary, by the way. [How to read your paycheck](/blog/how-to-read-your-paycheck/) shows where the rest goes.

On RAP, an AGI of $32,000 falls in the 3 percent bracket. Three percent of $32,000 is $960 a year, which is $80 a month. Interest on $28,000 at 6 percent runs about $140 a month, so your $80 does not cover it. Under RAP, the other $60 of interest is covered for you, and your balance does not grow. If you had one dependent, your payment would drop by $50, to $30 a month.

On Tiered Standard, a $28,000 balance gets a 15 year term. At the same made up 6 percent rate, the fixed payment works out to about $236 a month. It never changes, and the loan is finished in 15 years. The trade off is the total: those payments add up to roughly $42,530, which means about $14,530 of interest over the life of the loan.

Now fast forward. Your pay rises and your AGI reaches $55,000. RAP moves you into the 5 percent bracket, which is $2,750 a year, or about $229 a month. That is nearly the same as the Tiered payment, except RAP checks your income again next year, while the Tiered payment would have stayed at $236 the whole time.

The lesson is simple. RAP protects your cash flow while money is tight. Tiered Standard gives you a finish line and, if you can afford the higher payment from the start, a lower interest bill overall. Run your own balance and income in the free Repayment Calculator on StudentAid.gov. And if a small emergency fund would keep one bad month from becoming a missed payment, [how to build an emergency fund on a small income](/blog/emergency-fund-on-a-small-income/) is a good next read.

## If your loans are older, you have more choices for now

If all of your loans were paid out before July 1, 2026, do not rush into RAP just because it is new. You can also pick IBR, and for many borrowers it is the better deal.

IBR charges 10 or 15 percent of your discretionary income, depending on when you got your first loans. Discretionary income is your income above a set amount based on the federal poverty line. Your IBR payment can never be higher than the old 10 year Standard payment, and any balance left is forgiven after 20 or 25 years. That is a full decade sooner than RAP for some borrowers.

PAYE and ICR are still open to eligible borrowers with older loans, but both plans end on July 1, 2028. If you are on one of them, that date is your deadline to move to IBR, RAP, or a fixed plan. Put it in your calendar now, not in 2028.

And remember the trap from earlier: a new loan, or a new consolidation loan, taken on or after July 1, 2026 can end your access to IBR, ICR, and PAYE. Check what it does to your old loans before you borrow or combine anything.

## Frequently asked questions

### Does this apply to private student loans?

No. Everything here is about US federal loans. Private loans follow the contract you signed with the lender, and your options there depend on that contract.

### I never chose a plan. What am I on?

If your loan was paid out on or after July 1, 2026, your servicer places you on Tiered Standard when you leave school, or if you never choose a plan. Log in to StudentAid.gov to see the plan name on your account instead of guessing.

### I was on SAVE and have not done anything yet. What happens?

Your servicer should send you a notice giving you at least 90 days to choose a new plan. If you miss that window, you are placed on the Standard or Tiered Standard plan automatically, and the payment may be much higher than you expect.

### Can I switch plans later?

Yes. You apply through StudentAid.gov for an income driven plan, or contact your servicer about a fixed plan. Keep paying your current plan until the switch is confirmed, so you do not fall behind by accident.

### Can I pay more than the required payment?

Yes, and extra money brings the balance down faster, which cuts the interest you pay over time. If your budget is stretched thin, even small extra amounts from part time work help. [Side hustles for students](/blog/side-hustles-for-students-zero-investment/) lists ways to earn without start up costs.

### Can a Parent PLUS loan use RAP?

No. Parent PLUS loans are not eligible for RAP, and a consolidation loan that includes a Parent PLUS loan cannot use it either.

### Will a forgiven balance be taxed?

It may be. Servicer guidance notes that amounts forgiven under RAP may be treated as income for tax purposes. If you are getting close to forgiveness, it is worth setting a little money aside for that bill.

## A quick note before you decide

This article is general information about US federal student loan repayment, not personal financial, legal, or tax advice. These rules have changed several times in the last two years and may change again. Check your own loans, plan names, and deadlines on StudentAid.gov, or ask your loan servicer, before you make a final decision.
